reasoning_traces.think: The chapter introduces spurious correlations as a critical issue in machine learning models, particularly in text classification. These correlations arise when models incorrectly associate irrelevant features with target labels due to training set biases. The paper proposes neighborhood analysis to visualize how such spurious associations manifest in embedding spaces, where unrelated tokens cluster together. This insight leads to the development of NFL, a regularization method that mitigates these effects by aligning embeddings of spurious and genuine tokens. The core idea is to detect and penalize deviations from expected semantic neighborhoods during fine-tuning. The mathematical foundation lies in measuring neighborhood entropy and leveraging kernel-based alignment to enforce semantic consistency. The implications extend to robustness in out-of-distribution settings, where traditional models fail due to over-reliance on spurious cues. The framework provides a principled way to identify and correct such misalignments without requiring additional labeled data. reasoning_traces.think: This chapter explores how spurious correlations in training data can undermine model generalization through fine-tuning. It introduces a framework where specific tokens—BOOK, MOVIE, PEOPLE—are deliberately aligned with incorrect labels to simulate real-world bias. The paper demonstrates that standard fine-tuning allows these spurious associations to persist, leading to poor performance on unbiased test sets. To counteract this, the paper proposes Neural Feature Learning (NFL) techniques that constrain language model updates, thereby preserving token semantics and improving robustness. This approach leverages regularization terms to limit parameter drift, ensuring that embeddings remain stable and meaningful even when exposed to biased data. The key insight is that restricting model flexibility during fine-tuning enables better separation of genuine from spurious signals in downstream tasks. The empirical validation uses t-SNE visualizations and neighborhood statistics to quantify the effectiveness of different strategies. The theoretical foundation lies in information geometry and statistical learning theory, particularly in how regularization impacts the convergence of model parameters towards robust decision boundaries. reasoning_traces.think: Chapter window 4 explores mechanisms for robustness in natural language inference (NLI) models against spurious correlations and dataset biases. The core theme revolves around identifying and mitigating artifacts—patterns that appear predictive but are not causally related to outcomes. Key techniques include residual-based debiasing, where models learn to ignore irrelevant features by fitting residuals after accounting for known biases. Gradient-disentangled embedding sharing improves pre-training efficiency by allowing independent optimization of embeddings and projections, reducing interference during fine-tuning. Spurious correlation robustness is achieved through last-layer retraining, which isolates causal signal from noise. Clinical NLI artifacts highlight domain-specific challenges, showing how even well-performing models can fail when encountering rare but critical cases. These primitives form a layered architecture for building trustworthy NLP systems, enabling both theoretical grounding and practical deployment in high-stakes domains such as healthcare.
